passages.context: Section 10 opens Anthony's second division with Luke 17:12-14. Allegorically, the ten lepers signify humanity's sin against the Decalogue and Christ cleanses infidelity and iniquity by the blood of redemption and the water of Baptism. Morally, the lepers signify sinners marked by five kinds and five bodily or domestic locations of leprosy, which the following sections expound as forms and manifestations of vice.
passages.notes: Read in the exact Centro Studi Latin PDF with its local apparatus and the beginning of the following development. This is a verified witness to Anthony's medieval reception of Luke 17 and Leviticus 13-14, not evidence of a later missal compiler's historical intent. passages.context: Section 13 reads Christ's command in three ordered terms: ite signifies contrition of heart, ostendite confession of the mouth, and sacerdotibus satisfaction in works. Anthony develops the prodigal son's rising and going, the penitent's shame and ordered self-accusation, confession to priests entrusted with binding and loosing, and cleansing in contrition together with a firm purpose of confessing.
passages.notes: Read in the exact Centro Studi Latin PDF through the complete section and its source apparatus. The modern note to Anthony's sentence about cleansing in contrition says that the precise formulation does not occur in its cited Peter Lombard locus and supplies related Cassiodoran and Augustinian material; do not present the sentence as an exact Lombard quotation. The section witnesses Anthony's penitential exegesis and does not by itself replace a complete doctrinal account of the sacrament. passages.context: Sections 15-18 expound the healed Samaritan's return, prostration, and thanksgiving. Anthony calls him Samaritanus, id est custos: he safeguards received good by attributing it to God rather than himself. Falling on his face expresses shame and humble self-knowledge; thanksgiving renders praise to the giver of every good. Anthony joins unus, Samaritanus, and alienigena to unity, humility's keeping, and evangelical poverty, then answers them with surge, vade, and fides tua te salvum fecit and closes by relating the return to the fruits of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23.
passages.notes: Read across all four numbered sections in the exact Centro Studi Latin PDF, including their source notes. work.description: Anthony of Padua's sermon for the Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost, a constituent of his Sermons for Sundays and Festivals. Its three principal divisions receive Luke 17:11-19 alongside Galatians 5:16-24 and passages from Job.
